title: The Bride of Wood and Glass: Buenos Aires, the Arlberg, and a Grave That Outgrew Its Occupant
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Barrio Norte, Buenos Aires: the only child
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January
stops.campa: In 1944 a daughter is born to the Crociati family in the blocks north of the Plaza Francia, the only child of a father who dresses the hair of Buenos Aires society and a mother with an artist's eye and no gallery to put it in. No clinic is named in any record. No street number survives. What survives is the class she is born into: Italian by descent, porteña by address, close enough to Recoleta that the cemetery wall is a short walk from the family door. They call her Liliana.
suggested_refs: Baptismal and civil registers of the Recoleta parishes for 1944, not located
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Tumba de Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (birth year, only child, parents' occupations)
Neighbourhood pin is a proxy; no address is attested

stops.name: Avenida Alvear, Recoleta: the salon
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed decade; the trade is attested, the premises are not
stops.campa: Her father works the avenue where the ateliers stand between the embassies and the cemetery gate, cutting and setting the hair of women who come in by appointment and leave rearranged. Liliana grows up inside that business of appearances, among combs and pins and the long practised patience of being looked at, and the women in his chair learn her name before she is anyone in her own right. That he is a hairdresser to Buenos Aires society is attested. Where he worked is not: no street number for any salon of his has been located.
suggested_refs: Commercial registers of Avenida Alvear salons, 1950s, not located
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Tumba de Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (father a noted society hairdresser)
Street location inferred from where such ateliers clustered

stops.name: Barrio Norte, Buenos Aires: the School of Fine Arts
stops.date_confidence: enrolment attested as a phrase only; no year is given in any source
stops.campa: She studies Bellas Artes. The detail arrives late and sideways, from her husband's family speaking to a cemetery historian fifty years afterward, and it changes the shape of what is known: she is a student of art before she is ever a subject of it. Among her fellow students is a friend whose face will one day be given to her bronze. No enrolment record has been found, no dated matriculation, no drawing and no canvas of her own hand. What is recorded is two words: estudiaba Bellas Artes.
stops.quote_source: recoletacemetery.com/?p=646, from testimony supplied by the Szaszak family
suggested_refs: Matriculation rolls of the Buenos Aires Escuela Nacional de Bellas Artes, early 1960s
sources: recoletacemetery.com/?p=646 (family testimony)
Supersedes an earlier reconstruction of convent schooling, now withdrawn

stops.name: Teatro Colón, Buenos Aires: the season
stops.date_confidence: speculative venue; no source places her here on any date
stops.campa: No programme has surfaced with her name printed in it, and nothing located places her inside this building on any evening. The theatre is included as the era's characteristic occasion for porteño society, not as a night anyone can date. She is nineteen in 1963 by the tomb's reckoning and seventeen by the newspaper's. That society runs on seasons. The daughters of her set are presented to the city under the gold and the red of the Colón, the boxes full, the aisles a slow parade of families checking each other's children.
suggested_refs: Teatro Colón season programmes and society columns, early 1960s
sources: No primary source locates Liliana Crociati at the Teatro Colón
Included as the era's characteristic venue for porteño society occasions

stops.name: Alvear Palace Hotel, Recoleta: the engagement
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; courtship undocumented, dated backward from the wedding
stops.campa: Two blocks from the ground where she will be buried, the hotel on Avenida Alvear keeps the ballroom in which engagements of her circle are announced. Somewhere in that circle she meets Janos Szaszak, a Hungarian whom everyone calls Jancsi. No society column names the meeting and no source gives a date for it; the courtship is dated backward from the wedding and from nothing else. She is twenty-two by the age cut into her tomb, or twenty by the age the newspaper will give. The wedding is set for October of the following year.
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires society columns, 1965-1966, for an engagement notice
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Tumba de Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (husband named as Janos 'Jancsi' Szaszak)
Venue and courtship are reconstruction; no source attests either

stops.name: Basílica del Pilar, Recoleta: the wedding
stops.date_confidence: date attested from family testimony; the church is an unattested guess
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of October 1966 Liliana Crociati marries Janos Szaszak. The date comes from her husband's family, given to a cemetery historian decades afterward. The church does not. The Pilar is the obvious candidate, the white basilica at the cemetery gate where weddings of means in this parish were held, and it is named here as a guess and nothing firmer. She wears a dress that will be described ever after as the one cast in bronze. Photographs her family later supplied show that it is not.
suggested_refs: Parish registers of Nuestra Señora del Pilar and neighbouring Recoleta parishes, October 1966
sources: recoletacemetery.com/?p=646 (marriage date 17 October 1966; the dress not an exact replica)
Wedding venue unattested in any source consulted

stops.name: Plaza Hotel, Buenos Aires: the reception
stops.date_confidence: speculative venue; no ledger or guest list located
stops.campa: If the wedding follows the pattern of her circle the party moves to the Plaza, under the mansard roof above the Plaza San Martín, waiters working between tables of relatives. Somebody makes a speech and nobody writes it down. No guest list and no hotel ledger has been located, nor any photograph of the night. What follows is three years and four months of marriage, about which the record is nearly silent. October in Buenos Aires is warm, and the season is beginning.
suggested_refs: Plaza Hotel function ledgers, October 1966
sources: No primary source confirms a reception venue
Included as period-typical reconstruction for a porteño society wedding

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the four married years
stops.date_confidence: period bracket 1966-1970; no dated event within it is attested
stops.campa: They are married three years and four months, and across that span the record goes silent. No address, no work, no children are attested. Almost every retelling of what happens next calls the trip to the Alps a honeymoon, which it cannot be, the wedding being more than three years behind them. The error travels well because a bride killed on her wedding journey is a better story than a married couple taking a winter holiday. The married couple on the winter holiday is what the record supports.
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires municipal and electoral records, 1966-1970, for a Szaszak household
sources: recoletacemetery.com/?p=646 (marriage date, against which the 'honeymoon' framing fails)
en.wikipedia.org, 'Tomb of Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (repeats the honeymoon framing)

stops.name: Ezeiza, Buenos Aires: the flight out
stops.date_confidence: month reconstructed from the arrival in the Alps; no departure date attested
stops.campa: They fly out of Ezeiza, the only door Argentina has to the wider world in 1970, in the middle of a porteño summer, bound for snow. No airline, no ticket, no hour of departure survives in anything located. What is known is where the holiday begins, and it is not Austria: they go first to the French Alps, to Val d'Isère. They are four years married and travelling as such, whatever the retellings say. She walks out onto the apron in February heat. She comes back through this airport in March in a hold.
suggested_refs: Aerolíneas Argentinas and Iberia passenger manifests, February 1970
sources: recoletacemetery.com/?p=646 (holiday begins at Val d'Isère, French Alps)
Departure airport inferred; Ezeiza was Argentina's only international gateway

stops.name: Galeão, Rio de Janeiro: the first refuelling
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed leg; no document places this couple on this route
stops.campa: If they fly the route Argentines flew to Europe that year, the aircraft sets down first at Galeão, taking on fuel under a different heat before the long haul over the Atlantic. Four hours north of Buenos Aires the cabin empties onto a hot apron and fills again; she may never have left her seat. Nothing ties this couple to this runway. The leg is here because the aircraft of 1970 could not cross without stopping, and because the corridor north from Buenos Aires ran through Rio, then Dakar, then Madrid, in that order.
suggested_refs: Route timetables for the Buenos Aires to Europe corridor, 1970
sources: No primary source documents any flight leg of this journey
Standard 1970-era stop on the Buenos Aires to Europe route

stops.name: Yoff, Dakar: the pause between continents
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed leg; unattested for this journey
stops.campa: Dakar is the forced pause on the westernmost point of Africa, where South Atlantic flights took on fuel before turning north for Europe. The runway at Yoff exists for exactly this, an aircraft that cannot yet reach Europe from South America in a single movement. No manifest names her here. The stop belongs to the era's flight patterns and not to any document of this journey, and it is placed on that basis. Tarmac, heat, an hour on the ground, then the climb out.
suggested_refs: Yoff airport traffic records, February 1970
sources: No primary source documents this leg
Characteristic refuelling stop on 1970 South Atlantic routes

stops.name: Barajas, Madrid: continental ground
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed leg; unattested for this journey
stops.campa: Madrid is where South American flights of the period first touch continental ground, and from Barajas a connection carries travellers on toward the mountains. Spain in February, a terminal at first light, a connection to be found. No boarding pass, no itinerary, no record of any leg of this trip has been located. Everything between Ezeiza and the snow is inference from how the route was flown, and it is held loosely. The documented part of the journey resumes only when they reach the Alps.
suggested_refs: Barajas transit records, February 1970
sources: No primary source documents this leg
Madrid was the era's typical connecting point for Argentina to Europe travel

stops.name: Val d'Isère, Savoie: where the holiday begins
stops.date_confidence: location attested from family testimony; arrival date unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The holiday begins in the French Alps, at Val d'Isère, in a February deep in the season. Savoie that winter is full of Europeans and a few South Americans with money and time. This is attested, from the husband's family, and it corrects nearly every account in circulation, which puts them in Austria from the first day. At some point in the weeks that follow they move east, across the border, toward the Arlberg. Why does a couple leave a French resort in mid-season for another country? No source located answers it.
suggested_refs: Hotel registers of Val d'Isère, February 1970
sources: recoletacemetery.com/?p=646 (the trip began at Val d'Isère in the French Alps)

stops.name: Landeck, Tyrol: the narrowing valley
stops.date_confidence: route town, not an attested stop; conditional on an approach from the east
stops.campa: The road to the Arlberg from the east runs through Landeck, a market town under its own castle at the point where the wide Inn valley narrows. If they came to Zürs by way of Innsbruck they passed through here; if they came up from France by another road they did not. No vehicle and no border crossing has been documented, and the town is on the map for the sake of the geography and carries no claim at all about the travellers. Snow is banked to the eaves, and above the town the pass road is worked open again every morning.
suggested_refs: Road and rail geography of the Arlberg approaches, 1970
sources: No primary source documents this leg
Landeck lies on the Innsbruck to St Anton to Flexenpass road toward Zürs

stops.name: Zürs am Arlberg, Vorarlberg: the avalanche
stops.date_confidence: date attested; the village is attested from family testimony and disputed by the encyclopaedia
stops.campa: In the night the mountain above Zürs lets go. The avalanche covers the hotel and comes through the window of their second-floor room while the two of them are asleep, and the snow arrives complete, filling the space in the time it takes to wake. It does not level the building. It finds one window. Accounts repeated for fifty years put this hotel sixty-four kilometres west of Innsbruck, in the Paznaun; the family places it in Vorarlberg, on the far side of the Arlberg, and the distance is nearer ninety.
stops.quote: On 26 Feb 1970, an avalanche covered their hotel & broke through their second story room window
suggested_refs: Austrian press and Lawinenwarndienst records for the Arlberg and Paznaun avalanches of 26 February 1970, not consulted
sources: recoletacemetery.com/?p=646 (Zürs am Arlberg; date; second-storey window)
es.wikipedia.org, 'Tumba de Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (second-floor window, night of 26 Feb 1970, hotel 64 km west of Innsbruck)
Contradiction between the two locations is recorded, not resolved

stops.name: Zürs am Arlberg: Jancsi is dug out
stops.date_confidence: attested; hour unknown
stops.campa: Janos Szaszak is taken out of the snow with hypothermia, warmed, and recovers within days. The cold that nearly takes him is the ordinary hazard of the mountain and is treated as such, with blankets and a warm room. He is the one the mountain gives back. What he does over the hours that follow is the only decision anyone in this story is recorded as making: he goes down the valley behind his wife, and when the doctors tell him what they have, he authorizes them to stop. He signs. He lives another twenty-six years.
suggested_refs: Rescue reports of the Zürs avalanche, 26 February 1970
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Tumba de Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (hypothermia, quickly reversed)
recoletacemetery.com/?p=646 (authorized removal of life support; died 1996)

stops.name: Zürs am Arlberg: Liliana is dug out
stops.date_confidence: attested that she was recovered alive; hour and circumstances unrecorded
stops.campa: Liliana is taken out alive and gravely injured, in a village with no hospital equal to what she needs, by men working in lamplight. The hour she is reached is not recorded, nor the name of anyone who reached her, nor anything said in that room. She is twenty-six by the age cut into her tomb and twenty-four by the notice La Nación runs the following day, and the two numbers have never been reconciled against a birth certificate. She has been married three years and four months.
suggested_refs: La Nación, Buenos Aires, death notice of 27 February 1970, seen only in transcription
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Tumba de Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (severe injuries)
recoletacemetery.com/?p=646 (recovered alive; La Nación gives her age as 24 against the tomb's 26)

stops.name: Innsbruck, the clinic on the Anichstrasse: 27 February
stops.date_confidence: attested from the dated obituary
stops.campa: She is flown down out of the mountains to the university clinic on the Anichstrasse and does not wake. The doctors declare her brain dead. On the twenty-seventh of February 1970, the day after the avalanche, her husband gives his permission and the machines are stopped. The Spanish account that has her dying days later, and the English one that has her killed outright in the hotel bed, are both wrong against the obituary her own family read in Buenos Aires that same week.
suggested_refs: Landeskrankenhaus Innsbruck admission and death records, February 1970
sources: recoletacemetery.com/?p=646, quoting the La Nación obituary of 27 February 1970
es.wikipedia.org (airlifted to Innsbruck, died 'days later')
en.wikipedia.org (death at the hotel), contradicted

stops.name: Barrio Norte, Buenos Aires: the news
stops.date_confidence: the notice is dated; the scene in the apartment is reconstruction
stops.campa: The news reaches a father who cuts hair and a mother who draws. After it reaches them, neither is ever described in any source as recovering, and what the record holds of the rest of their lives is a monument, built slowly, and then their own burial inside it. There is no transcript of the telephone call or the cable that carried the news across the Atlantic, and no account at all of that apartment on that day. La Nación carries the notice on the twenty-seventh of February.
suggested_refs: La Nación, 27 February 1970, page of death notices
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Tumba de Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (both parents lost interest in life; buried with her)
The notification scene itself is reconstruction

stops.name: Kranebitten, Innsbruck: the repatriation
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; no repatriation document located, month defaulted
stops.campa: Her body is prepared for the long way back and leaves Austria through the airport under the mountains at Kranebitten. Repatriation of a foreign national in 1970 is consulates and paperwork and a sealed casket, a hold rather than a cabin, and it is slow: a body crossing a border needs more documents than a living passenger and moves at the speed of the slowest of them. She crosses the Atlantic a second time within three weeks of crossing it the first. No manifest and no carrier's name has been located, and no date.
suggested_refs: Argentine consular repatriation files, Vienna or Munich, March 1970
sources: No primary source documents repatriation logistics
Reconstructed from the fact of her burial in Buenos Aires

stops.name: Ezeiza, Buenos Aires: the casket
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; arrival undocumented, month defaulted
stops.campa: The casket comes back through Ezeiza, onto the runway she left from in February. Buenos Aires in early March is still summer, and the heat on the apron is the same heat she flew out into. Her mother and father are there to meet it, and from this point neither of them is recorded doing anything except grieving and building. Nothing located gives the flight number or the hour, and no photograph of the arrival survives. Customs clears a coffin the way it clears any consignment, by paperwork.
suggested_refs: Ezeiza customs and cargo records, March 1970
sources: No primary source documents the arrival
Reconstructed as the counterpart of the Ezeiza departure

stops.name: Basílica del Pilar, Recoleta: the funeral mass
stops.date_confidence: speculative venue and date; neither is attested
stops.campa: If the wedding was held here, then the funeral closes the circle in the same nave three years and four months later, the same families in the same pews dressed for the opposite occasion. Neither venue is documented; both are guesses made from the same assumption. A mass was said somewhere in these blocks in March 1970, and the geography is the only part of the day that can be vouched for at all. The basilica stands two hundred metres from the grave, close enough that the mourners could walk it.
suggested_refs: Funeral notices in the Buenos Aires press, March 1970
sources: No primary source confirms the funeral venue
Offered as reconstruction paired with the equally unconfirmed wedding venue

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta, Buenos Aires: the burial
stops.date_confidence: burial attested; exact date not recorded, month defaulted
stops.campa: She goes into the ground at La Recoleta among admirals and presidents and the founding families of the city, in a cemetery three centuries into the business of housing them. There is nothing yet to see. A plot, a temporary marker, the narrow stone streets of shut vaults on either side. The Crociati name is not among the great ones cut into the avenues here. The chapel that will bring strangers here by the busload does not exist. Her mother has already begun to think about it.
suggested_refs: Internment records of the Cementerio de la Recoleta, March 1970
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Tomb of Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (body returned to Argentina and interred at La Recoleta)
es.wikipedia.org, 'Tumba de Liliana Crociati de Szaszak'

segments.name: The Chapel of Wood and Glass

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the mother draws it herself
stops.date_confidence: authorship attested; no date for the design is given in any source
stops.campa: Her mother does not commission the tomb. She designs it herself, a neo-Gothic chapel of wood and glass with arches and broad stained panels, built to let light fall inside rather than to keep the dead in the dark. Grief becomes a problem with dimensions and materials and a client of one. She is not an architect, and no source located calls her one. How long the drawings take is not recorded, nor whether the father had any say in them. No source in Spanish or in English gives a date for the design.
suggested_refs: Construction permits and plans lodged with the Cementerio de la Recoleta administration, 1970-1972
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Tumba de Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (the mother, an artist, designed the neo-Gothic mausoleum)

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the chapel goes up
stops.date_confidence: no construction or completion date is attested; year is an inference from the burial
stops.campa: Masons fit a Gothic front into a plot no wider than its neighbours and glaziers set panels bright enough to read as light rather than as wall. The chapel goes up taller and more open than anything around it. Wood in a cemetery of stone is a maintenance problem, and the mother chooses it anyway. The custom of this cemetery, formalized when the city walled and paved it into avenues in the 1880s, is a closed door of marble, and this one can be seen into. No completion date appears in any source consulted.
suggested_refs: Photographic surveys of the Recoleta avenues, early 1970s
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Tumba de Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (large stained-glass windows, neo-Gothic, abundant light)
en.wikipedia.org, 'Tomb of Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (contrast with surrounding monuments)

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: Viladrich casts the bride
stops.date_confidence: 1972 inherited from the sculptor's own file; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Wilfredo Viladrich casts her life-size in bronze, standing, in a wedding dress, an engagement ring on her hand. The family gives him photographs. The dress he makes is not an exact copy of the one she wore, and the face is not hers either but a portrait of a friend from her years at the School of Fine Arts. The bride at the edge of the grave is a composite, assembled out of the people who knew her, and almost nobody who stops to photograph it knows that. The casting is dated 1972.
stops.quote_source: recoletacemetery.com/?p=646, on the dress, from photographs supplied by the family
suggested_refs: Studio records of Wilfredo Viladrich for the Crociati commission
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Tomb of Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (life-size bronze, wedding dress, engagement ring; sculptor 'Wilfredo Viladrich')
es.wikipedia.org gives 'Wílfredo Viladrich'; earlier working material gave 'Wifredo', flagged
recoletacemetery.com/?p=646 (dress not an exact replica; face a friend's; no sculptor named)

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: A Mia Figlia
stops.date_confidence: authorship attested; no date for the plaque is given
stops.campa: Her father sets a plaque beneath the statue with a poem on it, in Italian, titled for her. He writes it himself, in the language of his own parents rather than the one his daughter was schooled in. Nothing on the tomb translates it, and no translation was ever fixed to the stone, so that visitors who cannot read Italian walk past the only words in this cemetery written by a man buried three metres behind them. The poem asks the same question from its first line onward and never answers it: solo mi chiedo il perché.
stops.quote: Solo mi chiedo il perché / Tu se partita e distrutto hai lasciato il mio cuore.
stops.quote_source: 'A Mia Figlia', opening lines, as reproduced in full on en.wikipedia, 'Tomb of Liliana Crociati de Szaszak'
suggested_refs: The plaque itself, and the full Italian text with translation at en.wikipedia
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Tomb of Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (full Italian text and English translation of the poem)
Corrects earlier working material claiming no copy of the text existed outside the tomb

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the father
stops.date_confidence: year unknown and unattested; placeholder only, sources say only 'some years later'
stops.campa: He dies some years after her, and no source located gives the year. He is buried in the tomb he wrote for, behind the plaque with his own lines on it, so that the tomb becomes a building he furnished with verse and then moved into. He had been a hairdresser to a whole city and a poet exactly once. What the record says about him afterward is a single clause: that both parents lost interest in living after Innsbruck and did not get it back. Nobody in the family was interviewed for fifty years.
suggested_refs: Cementerio de la Recoleta internment ledgers for the Crociati vault, 1970s-1980s
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Tumba de Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (parents died years later and were buried alongside their daughter)
Death year not attested in any source consulted

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the mother
stops.date_confidence: year unknown and unattested; placeholder only
stops.campa: The mother is buried inside her own building. She chose the glass and the pitch of the arches and the wood that no other vault on this avenue uses, and she is carried in through the door she drew. The artist is interred in the artwork, and the neo-Gothic front is the only work of hers that anyone can point to. Her death year is not attested in any source consulted, in Spanish or in English. What the sources carry is a clause: parents buried alongside their daughter.
suggested_refs: Cementerio de la Recoleta internment ledgers for the Crociati vault
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Tumba de Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (parents buried alongside their daughter)
Death year not attested

stops.name: Barrio Norte, Buenos Aires: the dog in the apartment
stops.date_confidence: the dog's existence is attested; nothing about his life is dated
stops.campa: Sabú is her dog, alive before any of this, in the apartment in Barrio Norte. Nothing describes him. No breed is given, no age, no photograph is reproduced in any source located. The name is spelled Sabú, and that is the whole of what the record holds about him while he is alive. He outlives her by many years, which is what the husband's family stated plainly in 2021 and which almost nobody repeats. In the meantime he is a dog in a house where the daughter does not come home.
suggested_refs: Family photographs of Sabú, referenced but not published
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Tomb of Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (Sabú her living companion)
recoletacemetery.com, 2021 update at post 312 (Sabú died many years after Liliana)

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the story told at the graveside
stops.date_confidence: undated tradition; the placeholder year carries no claim
stops.campa: The story told at the graveside is that Sabú died of grief on the day of her funeral, refused food until his heart stopped, and was buried with her, and that this is why a dog is sculpted into a human tomb in a cemetery that permits no such thing. Guides tell it. Travel writing repeats it. It is false, and the family said so. The legend holds because the bronze is arranged to support it: her hand on his head, the two of them facing out together down the avenue.
suggested_refs: Recoleta guiding scripts and travel writing carrying the grief-death legend
sources: Tradition repeated in tourist and cemetery-guide accounts
recoletacemetery.com, 2021 update at post 312, family testimony refuting it

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the second bronze
stops.date_confidence: no date located for the second casting; year is a placeholder
stops.campa: After the dog dies, Viladrich casts him too and sets him at her side, and only then is the group finished: the bride, the dog, the hand on his head. The second casting matches the first in scale and in patina, done by the same hand. What visitors read as a single frozen moment took two castings and an unrecorded number of years between them. No date has been found for the second bronze. What is certain is the order, and the order is the reverse of the story everyone tells. She goes first. The dog is added to her.
suggested_refs: Foundry records for the second Viladrich casting
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Tomb of Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (the dog cast and added after his death)
Date of the second casting not attested

stops.name: Buenos Aires: Janos Szaszak's remaining years
stops.date_confidence: death year attested; the place is not, and the pin is a default
stops.campa: Janos Szaszak lives another twenty-six years. He is the only person to come out of that hotel room, and he does not appear to have spoken publicly about it; where he lived after 1970 is not stated in anything located. He was a husband for three years and four months and a widower for a matter of months. He marries a woman called Trixie and has two children. The account of those years comes from his own children, given to a cemetery historian in 2021. He dies in 1996.
suggested_refs: Civil records for Janos Szaszak after 1970, country unknown
sources: recoletacemetery.com/?p=646 (remarried Trixie, two children, died 1996)
Place of residence after 1970 not attested; pin defaults to Buenos Aires

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the snout
stops.date_confidence: present-day condition; the date is a marker, not an event
stops.campa: The bronze has gone the dull green of old alloy everywhere except the dog's nose, which is gold, rubbed back to bare metal by hands. The luck is not attached to any saint or any story, only to the dog. None of this was planned by the mother who drew the chapel or by the father who wrote the poem, and it is now the most reliable thing that happens at this grave. Tour groups stop here; guides point out the dress, the glass, the plaque nobody translates aloud, and one after another the visitors put a hand on the snout on the way past.
suggested_refs: Conservation surveys of the Viladrich bronzes at Recoleta
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Tumba de Liliana Crociati de Szaszak' (belief that touching the dog's snout brings luck; the polished metal)

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: catalogued to the second of arc
stops.date_confidence: present-day record; the date is a marker, not an event
stops.campa: The tomb has been catalogued down to the second of arc: 34 degrees 35 minutes 18 seconds south, 58 degrees 23 minutes 35 seconds west, sharing its stretch of pathway with the vault of R. Fuchs-Ritrovato. Photographers file it under her name, in a cemetery where being photographed is most of the afterlife on offer. It sits a few rows from presidents and a short walk from the black granite the whole world queues for. The pathway is narrow enough that two people cannot pass without one of them turning sideways.

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: no biography
stops.date_confidence: present-day state of the record
stops.campa: There is no biography of Liliana Crociati de Szaszak. The encyclopaedia article is titled for the tomb and not for the woman, and it describes her only through the monument, which is the only place she is described at length by anyone. Her name survives attached to a building rather than to a body of work or a career. Say the name in Recoleta and a guide will point at the statue. Twenty-six years of a life, or twenty-four, come down to a bronze dress that is not her dress and a face that is not her face.
